chunks.text: 2.2 Long-sequence modeling in pathology Transformer and interventional MIL extend independent pooling through contextual dependency and confounder-aware bag learning [ 9 , 19 ] . Graph-based models encode relational or spatial context through tissue graphs [ 20 , 21 ] . Hierarchical models aggregate local-to-slide representations across scales [ 22 , 23 ] . Attention-based models can be computationally expensive for large bags, whereas graph and hierarchical models depend on relation construction or multi-scale design choices. Structured state space and Mamba models offer a linear-time long-sequence alternative, with Mamba and VMamba establishing selective/state-space operators [ 10 , 24 ] . S4MIL and MambaMIL adapt this direction to WSI sequences [ 25 , 11 ] . SemaMIL combines semantic reordering with retrieval-guided state-space modeling [ 12 ] ; its sequence-construction strategy complements the study of parallel contextual streams. MambaMIL is the closest sequence-side comparator to LEAF-Mamba [ 11 ] . 2.3 Pathology foundation models and representation mismatch Pathology foundation models improve frozen patch representations: CTransPath uses pathology-specific contrastive pretraining, and PLIP adds vision-language supervision [ 26 , 27 ] . Broader general-purpose and clinical-grade encoders expand transfer across pathology tasks [ 7 , 8 ] . Recent multimodal whole-slide encoders extend this trend with image-text supervision [ 28 , 29 ] . FG-PAN refines visual patches and aligns them with fine-grained descriptions for zero-shot brain tumor subtyping [ 30 ] . MeDKCoOp uses graph-structured visual and textual knowledge for biomedical prompt adaptation [ 31 ] . Both study how reusable vision-language representations can be matched to domain-specific evidence. Frozen representations can still benefit from downstream task adaptation, as investigated by RRTMIL [ 13 ] .

The feature mismatch addressed by this adaptation is distinct from generalization to a new acquisition domain. The comparison of interest is how the adaptation objective and aggregation operators contribute under the same frozen-feature protocol. 3 Method LEAF-Mamba transforms frozen patch embeddings, models them through long-range and sequence-local paths, and combines the resulting features before gated attention pooling. The adapter and aggregator are trained jointly with slide-level supervision, while the patch encoder remains frozen. Figure 2 summarizes the complete pipeline. Figure 2: Overview of LEAF-Mamba. Frozen features undergo reconstruction-regularized latent evidence adaptation and Mamba-guided fusion of long-range sequence context, short-range token interactions, and content-dependent gating for slide-level prediction. 3.1 Problem Setup Following the standard MIL paradigm, the i i -th WSI is represented as a bag ℬ i = { x i ​ j } j = 1 N i , \mathcal{B}_{i}=\{x_{ij}\}_{j=1}^{N_{i}}, (1) where N i N_{i} is the number of patches and x i ​ j x_{ij} denotes a raw image patch. A frozen feature extractor maps each patch to h i ​ j ∈ ℝ D h_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} , producing a bag feature matrix H i ∈ ℝ N i × D H_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times D} . We denote the slide-level target by 𝒴 i \mathcal{Y}_{i} : for diagnostic classification, 𝒴 i = y i \mathcal{Y}_{i}=y_{i} with y i ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , C − 1 } y_{i}\in\{0,1,\ldots,C-1\} ; for survival prediction, 𝒴 i = ( t i , δ i ) \mathcal{Y}_{i}=(t_{i},\delta_{i}) contains the observed time and event indicator. The goal is to learn a mapping F ⁡ ( H i ) F(H_{i}) that produces class logits or a survival risk score from frozen bag features. 3.2 Latent Evidence Adaptation LEA formulates task-specific feature adaptation with an auxiliary reconstruction objective before aggregation. The input is the frozen feature matrix H i H_{i} , whose representation was learned before the downstream MIL task.

Slide-level supervision trains the adapter jointly with the aggregator; reconstructing H i H_{i} adds an input-recovery objective to the task loss. LEA projects each token into a lower-dimensional code from which a decoder reconstructs the original feature. The module contains a nonlinear encoder E ⁡ ( ⋅ ) E(\cdot) , a decoder G ⁡ ( ⋅ ) G(\cdot) , and a linear skip projection P skip ​ ( ⋅ ) P_{\mathrm{skip}}(\cdot) . We define the latent representation as Z i = E ⁡ ( H i ) + P skip ​ ( H i ) ∈ ℝ N i × d . Z_{i}=E(H_{i})+P_{\mathrm{skip}}(H_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times d}. (2) The encoder and decoder are lightweight projection heads applied token-wise, with E ⁡ ( h ) = W 2 E ​ ϕ ​ ( W 1 E ​ h ) , G ⁡ ( z ) = W 2 G ​ ϕ ​ ( W 1 G ​ z ) , E(h)=W^{E}_{2}\phi(W^{E}_{1}h),\quad G(z)=W^{G}_{2}\phi(W^{G}_{1}z), (3) where ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) is GELU and the latent width satisfies d < D d<D . The nonlinear encoder learns the task-adaptive transformation, while the linear skip projection supplies a second route from the frozen input. The decoder reconstructs the original feature matrix: H ^ i = G ⁡ ( Z i ) ∈ ℝ N i × D . \hat{H}_{i}=G(Z_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times D}. (4) The reconstruction loss is ℒ rec = 1 N i ​ ∑ j = 1 N i ‖ h i ​ j − h ^ i ​ j ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\frac{1}{N_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{i}}\left\|h_{ij}-\hat{h}_{ij}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (5) The overall objective is ℒ = ℒ task + λ rec ​ ℒ rec , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}, (6) where ℒ task \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}} is cross-entropy for diagnostic classification and the negative Cox partial log-likelihood for survival prediction. The task loss trains predictive features, and the reconstruction term penalizes input-recovery error. One stream models long-range dependencies, while the other captures interactions within a finite convolutional window. Combining these receptive fields follows the hybrid-operator design principle used in Conformer [ 34 ] . For coordinate-bearing bags, raster serialization sorts patch coordinates by y y first and then x x , preserving input order for exact ties. The ordered sequence is retained across blocks. Let Z i ( 0 ) = Z i Z_{i}^{(0)}=Z_{i} denote the input to the first evidence-fusion block. At block l l , we normalize the current token sequence: Z ~ i ( l − 1 ) = LN ⁡ ( Z i ( l − 1 ) ) . \tilde{Z}_{i}^{(l-1)}=\mathrm{LN}(Z_{i}^{(l-1)}). (7) The global stream uses a selective state space operation Φ SSM ​ ( ⋅ ) \Phi_{\mathrm{SSM}}(\cdot) to model long-range dependencies: Z global ( l ) = Φ SSM ​ ( Z ~ i ( l − 1 ) ) . Z_{\mathrm{global}}^{(l)}=\Phi_{\mathrm{SSM}}(\tilde{Z}_{i}^{(l-1)}). (8) Because Mamba-style models are sequence-order sensitive, we use the same coordinate-derived ordering for LEAF-Mamba and MambaMIL in all comparisons. Alongside the global stream, a separate local stream models short-range token interactions using depthwise separable convolutions: Z local ( l ) = ϕ ⁡ ( PWConv ⁡ ( DWConv k ​ ( Z ~ i ( l − 1 ) ) ) ) , Z_{\mathrm{local}}^{(l)}=\phi\left(\mathrm{PWConv}\left(\mathrm{DWConv}_{k}(\tilde{Z}_{i}^{(l-1)})\right)\right), (9) where DWConv k \mathrm{DWConv}_{k} is a depthwise one-dimensional convolution with kernel size k k , PWConv \mathrm{PWConv} is a pointwise convolution, and ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) is the GELU activation. The default kernel spans seven consecutive tokens in the raster-ordered sequence, defining a sequence-local receptive field . Convolutional windows follow this sequence across row transitions, tissue holes, and disconnected regions.

The kernel size determines the number of neighboring tokens processed at each position. 3.4 Content-Dependent Evidence Fusion Gated fusion combines the two evidence streams through input-dependent modulation of their joint representation. We first concatenate the two streams into U i ( l ) = [ Z local ( l ) ; Z global ( l ) ] ∈ ℝ N i × 2 ​ d U_{i}^{(l)}=[Z_{\mathrm{local}}^{(l)};Z_{\mathrm{global}}^{(l)}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{i}\times 2d} and apply a gated projection: Z fuse ( l ) = ( U i ( l ) ​ W proj ) ⊙ σ ⁡ ( U i ( l ) ​ W gate ) , Z_{\mathrm{fuse}}^{(l)}=(U_{i}^{(l)}W_{\mathrm{proj}})\odot\sigma(U_{i}^{(l)}W_{\mathrm{gate}}), (10) where W proj , W gate ∈ ℝ 2 ​ d × d W_{\mathrm{proj}},W_{\mathrm{gate}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d\times d} are learnable parameters, σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The sigmoid gate modulates the projected joint representation, allowing the fused feature to respond differently across slides and tokens. A residual feed-forward update then refines the representation: Z i ( l ) = Z i ( l − 1 ) + M ⁡ ( LN ⁡ ( Z i ( l − 1 ) + Z fuse ( l ) ) ) , Z_{i}^{(l)}=Z_{i}^{(l-1)}+M\left(\mathrm{LN}\left(Z_{i}^{(l-1)}+Z_{\mathrm{fuse}}^{(l)}\right)\right), (11) where Z i ( l − 1 ) Z_{i}^{(l-1)} and Z i ( l ) Z_{i}^{(l)} denote the block input and output, M ⁡ ( ⋅ ) M(\cdot) is an MLP, and LN ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{LN}(\cdot) denotes layer normalization. Gated attention pools the final normalized token sequence into a bag representation, which is passed to the slide-level task head. The kernel size determines the number of neighboring tokens processed at each position. 4 Experiments We organize the experiments around three questions.

First, does the representation-and-evidence design remain useful across feature extractors? Second, does the same principle carry from diagnostic classification to noisier survival prediction? Third, do controlled variants support the roles assigned to LEA, local modeling, and gated fusion? We first define the datasets and unified protocol, then answer these questions through benchmark comparisons and targeted ablations. 4.1 Datasets and Protocol We evaluate LEAF-Mamba on both diagnostic classification and survival prediction under a unified frozen-feature protocol. For diagnostic classification, we use EBRAINS for 30-class brain tumor subtyping [ 44 ] , BRACS for 7-class breast lesion classification [ 45 ] , and Camelyon16 for breast cancer metastasis detection [ 46 ] . BRACS is evaluated with both 5-fold cross-validation and its official split. For survival prediction, we use five cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA): BLCA, BRCA, COADREAD, STAD, and HNSC [ 47 ] . Prognostic performance is measured by Concordance Index (C-Index) and reported as C-Index × 100 \times 100 . 4.2 Implementation Details All reproduced baselines reuse the same pre-extracted features, split protocol, early-stopping rule, and metric computation as LEAF-Mamba. For Mamba-based models, the same fixed coordinate-derived patch serialization is used throughout so that ordering does not confound the comparison. This protocol isolates the slide-level aggregator stage under frozen features. LEAF-Mamba uses two evidence-fusion blocks unless otherwise stated. In the LEA module, the encoder maps the input dimension D D to a latent width d d through a hidden width of 2 ​ d 2d , uses layer normalization, GELU, and dropout 0.25 0.25 , and adds a linear skip projection from the frozen feature. The decoder mirrors this projection to reconstruct the original frozen feature and contributes the mean-squared reconstruction loss during training.

Each evidence-fusion block applies a local depthwise one-dimensional convolution with kernel size 7 7 , followed by a pointwise convolution, and a global Mamba path with state dimension 32 32 , convolution width 4 4 , and expansion factor 2 2 . The local and global outputs are concatenated, projected, and modulated by a sigmoid fusion gate before a residual feed-forward update. After the final block, gated attention pools the refined token features into a slide representation, which is passed to a linear task head. 4.3 Comparison with Recent WSI Baselines To present the extensive comparisons within the available space, Figure 4 uses a compact multi-panel layout showing score differences relative to the strongest baseline for each feature extractor. Tables 1 – 4 report the complete numerical results corresponding to Figure 4 . Figure 4: Diagnostic classification and TCGA survival prediction results across frozen feature extractors. The vertical axis shows the score difference from the best baseline using the same feature extractor, on a nonlinear scale. Figure 4 includes recent WSI baselines. The MHIM variants combine masked hard-instance mining with ABMIL or TransMIL backbones [ 48 ] . CAMIL and RPMIL provide context-aware and probabilistic WSI comparators, respectively [ 14 , 16 ] . ACMIL and the instance-jigsaw model provide attention-challenging and order-restoration comparators [ 15 , 17 ] . In Figure 4 , LEAF-Mamba achieves strongest average diagnostic performance for each feature extractor under shared frozen-feature protocol. Specifically, average AUC reaches 87.7, 88.5, and 89.4 with ResNet-50, PLIP, and CONCH v1.5 features, respectively, exceeding the strongest baseline, Jigsaw, by 1.1, 1.9, and 1.0 percentage points. This consistent ranking shows benefits across all three frozen feature extractors.

The BRACS official split provides a representative benchmark-level example: with PLIP features, LEAF-Mamba achieves AUC 77.8, exceeding Jigsaw’s 74.6 by 3.2 percentage points. Together, the average results and this task-specific comparison support the effectiveness of combining feature adaptation with sequence aggregation for diagnostic classification. Beyond diagnostic classification, Figure 4 shows that LEAF-Mamba also achieves the best average C-Index with each evaluated feature extractor. Across the five TCGA cohorts, the average C-Index × 100 \times 100 is 67.0 with ResNet-50 features and 67.3 with PLIP and CONCH v1.5 features. These scores exceed Jigsaw, the strongest survival baseline, by 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 points, respectively. The leading average performance across all three feature extractors complements the diagnostic results, showing that the combined adaptation and aggregation design is effective for both slide-level classification and survival prediction. This design therefore supports both prediction tasks evaluated here. Table 1: Diagnostic classification results with ResNet-50 features. All scores are percentages; higher is better. Higher is better (continued). Table 5 first isolates the aggregation design with LEA enabled. The global-only model achieves 76.8 AUC, 36.4 ACC, and 29.2 F1, exceeding the local-only model on all three metrics. Combining both branches through concatenation, addition, or averaging further improves all three scores over global-only aggregation. Input-dependent gated fusion achieves the highest scores of 78.6 AUC, 40.0 ACC, and 32.7 F1, improving on the global-only model by 1.8, 3.6, and 3.5 percentage points, respectively. Compared with the learned static gate, it gains 0.8 AUC, 2.1 ACC, and 1.4 F1 points. These comparisons support both the use of parallel long-range and sequence-local branches and input-dependent modulation of their joint representation. Table 6 compares adapters under global-only aggregation. Full LEA achieves 76.8 AUC, 36.4 ACC, and 29.2 F1, compared with 75.1, 34.4, and 27.4 for the frozen PCA bridge.

It matches the two-layer MLP in AUC while improving ACC and F1 by 0.3 and 0.9 points. In the BRACS branch comparison, parallel global–local processing improves on either branch alone, and input-dependent fusion further improves on a learned static gate. In the adapter comparison, removing reconstruction reduces performance, supporting the use of input recovery as an auxiliary training objective.

These results connect the design choices to their controlled variants: adaptation changes the features available to aggregation, while fusion changes how complementary sequence representations are combined. The cross-setting results also show that the contributions of the two components depend on the task and the aggregator. With PLIP features on BRACS, adaptation improves the gated global–local model but does not improve the global-only model’s AUC. For TCGA-BRCA, the adapted global-only variant slightly exceeds the complete model in C-Index. Thus, the strongest average benchmark performance of the complete framework does not imply that each component improves every setting. The evidence supports evaluating adaptation and aggregation jointly, with their individual contributions assessed under matched feature extractors and protocols. 5.2 Scope and Limitations Our study focuses on learning from frozen patch representations, enabling controlled comparisons of adaptation and aggregation across feature extractors. Within this setting, the information available to the model depends on the pretrained encoder; exploring selective encoder fine-tuning would help establish when adaptation at the feature level is sufficient and when updating the encoder offers additional benefits. In addition, local interactions are defined along a fixed coordinate-derived sequence. Comparing alternative spatial orderings and incorporating explicit two-dimensional relationships are promising directions for extending the fusion design. Finally, the current evaluation covers multiple public benchmarks, while transfer across institutions remains an important next step. Independent cohorts with different patient populations and slide preparation practices would help characterize the conditions under which the observed benefits generalize.

Independent cohorts with different patient populations and slide preparation practices would help characterize the conditions under which the observed benefits generalize. 6 Conclusion We presented LEAF-Mamba, a frozen-feature WSI framework combining reconstruction-regularized token adaptation, long-range sequence modeling, sequence-local convolution, and input-dependent fusion. Our aim was to address a central challenge in weakly supervised computational pathology: adapting pretrained patch representations to downstream tasks while bringing together complementary local and global information. Across feature extractors and prediction tasks, LEAF-Mamba achieves strong overall performance in both diagnostic classification and survival prediction. The component analyses further highlight the value of jointly designing feature adaptation and contextual aggregation. More broadly, these findings suggest that effective use of pathology foundation models depends on how their representations are adapted and integrated into slide-level decisions. This perspective offers a direction for connecting reusable pretrained features with diverse pathology tasks.

Future work will extend this approach to cross-institutional evaluation and multimodal learning, exploring how tissue representations can be combined with complementary patient information for more comprehensive disease characterization.
